summary: Extends the Babel routing protocol to announce routes to IPv4 prefixes with an IPv6 next hop. IPv4 traffic can then flow through interfaces with no IPv4 address assigned. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A road sign lists directions in one address style, even if you need a different one for the next turn.

ipv4 routes via ipv6 next hop
how does babel support ipv4 over ipv6 next hop

subtitle: Extending the Babel routing protocol to route IPv4 over IPv6 next hops

tldr.problem: IPv4 networks sometimes benefit from forwarding through routers that do not have IPv4 addresses assigned, using only IPv6 for their backbone infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: This extension to the Babel routing protocol adds a new Address Encoding (AE) that allows routers to announce IPv4 prefixes with IPv6 next hops, called v4-via-v6 routes.
tldr.outcome: Networks can operate with fewer IPv4 addresses while maintaining IPv4 connectivity, reducing manual configuration overhead.

today: RFC 9229 is an Experimental specification. It extends the Babel routing protocol to support a specific use case: networks with IPv6 cores and IPv4 edges. Implementations that support this extension can negotiate v4-via-v6 routes with each other, while remaining compatible with standard Babel implementations that ignore the new encoding.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
Routing protocols typically associate each route with a next hop address in the same address family as the destination prefix: IPv4 routes use IPv4 next hops, and IPv6 routes use IPv6 next hops. However, there is no fundamental technical reason for this restriction. An IPv4 packet can be routed through an IPv6 next hop just as easily as an IPv6 packet can be routed through an IPv4 next hop.

This is particularly useful for building networks with no IPv4 addresses in the core. The core routers can operate using only IPv6, while still providing IPv4 connectivity to edge hosts. This approach significantly reduces the amount of manual configuration required, since IPv6 link-local addresses can be autonomously configured without any static assignment. The RFC 5549 extension to BGP already demonstrated this idea; this RFC extends the Babel routing protocol with the same capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers in the middle of the network can use different address labels than the packets they are forwarding, as long as they can find the next router using their own labels.

sections.title: How v4-via-v6 Routes Work
sections.content:
The Babel protocol uses Address Encodings (AE) to tag network addresses and prefixes. This extension defines a new AE called v4-via-v6, assigned the value 4. It has the same prefix format as the standard IPv4 AE, but it signals that the next hop is IPv6 instead of IPv4.

When a Babel node announces a v4-via-v6 route, it first establishes an IPv6 next-hop address using the standard Babel mechanisms. It then sends an Update TLV with AE=4 containing the IPv4 prefix. Routers that receive this announcement compute the route parameters (prefix, metric, router-id) as they would for a normal IPv4 route, but take the next hop from the most recent IPv6 next-hop announcement. Routers that do not implement this extension simply ignore the announcements, maintaining full backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The router tags the packet with a label saying 'this is an IPv4 destination, but follow the IPv6 directions to get there.' Old routers just ignore this tag and don't use the route.

sections.title: Routing Requests and Address Constraints
sections.content:
Route and Seqno requests are used to request updates for specific prefixes. Since these requests are not tied to a particular next hop, there is no semantic difference between requesting IPv4 routes and v4-via-v6 routes. Therefore, nodes should not send requests with AE=4; instead, they should request with AE=1 (standard IPv4) and accept either ordinary IPv4 or v4-via-v6 announcements in response.

Critically, the v4-via-v6 AE is only allowed in TLVs that carry network prefixes (Updates and Requests). The Next Hop and IHU TLVs must not use AE=4, since these TLVs always carry neighbor addresses which must remain in the same address family as the announcing router's interface.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask for directions, you ask for the destination, not how to describe the directions. And the intermediate routers always use their own address style.

sections.title: ICMPv4 and Path MTU Discovery
sections.content:
A critical requirement emerges from enabling IPv4 forwarding on routers without IPv4 addresses: every Babel router that forwards IPv4 traffic must be able to originate ICMPv4 packets. This is essential for Path MTU Discovery (PMTU), which relies on intermediate routers sending ICMP 'Packet Too Big' messages when they encounter links that cannot carry a packet.

When a router has no IPv4 address available, it can use one of several mechanisms. If any interface has an assigned IPv4 address (other than loopback), that address can be used as the source of originated ICMPv4 packets. Alternatively, the experimental mechanism defined in RFC 7600 allows using the dummy address 192.0.0.8 as the source address. Note that using the same dummy address on multiple routers can hamper debugging tools like traceroute.
sections.plainLanguage: If a packet is too big for a link, the router must send a message back saying 'that did not fit.' Even if the router does not have its own address label, it needs a way to send those messages back.

sections.title: Protocol Encoding and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Prefixes tagged with AE 4 (v4-via-v6) are encoded and decoded identically to AE 1 (IPv4) prefixes, as defined in the base Babel specification. However, a distinct compression state is maintained for AE 4, separate from AE 1. This allows the protocol to use address compression efficiently without interfering with other address encodings.

The extension maintains full backward compatibility. Implementations that do not understand v4-via-v6 will silently ignore the new AE, leaving such routes unused. This is safe because the extension does not modify the format of any existing TLV or sub-TLV. The next-hop state used by v4-via-v6 routes is the same as that used by IPv6 routes (AE 2 and 3), so there is no compatibility issue there either. For maximum compatibility, nodes with an assigned IPv4 address should prefer ordinary IPv4 announcements when possible, ensuring that older routers can still learn the route.
sections.plainLanguage: The new system uses the same language as the old IPv4 system, but keeps its own copy of the conversation history. Old routers just skip over the parts they don't understand.
